docs.title: Definition
docs.text: AI Adoption Intensity Terciles is a methodology developed in the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study to categorize firms based on the intensity of their AI adoption, measured by the PEPM (AI Spend Per Employee) metric.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
1. Firms are classified as AI adopters when they have three consecutive months of at least $100 in AI vendor spending
  2. Adoption intensity is measured as monthly AI spend per employee (PEPM) over the first three months after adoption
  3. Among treated firms, PEPM values are sorted and divided into three equal groups (terciles):
  4. High intensity: top tercile (most intensive AI adopters)
  5. Medium intensity: middle tercile
  6. Low intensity: bottom tercile (least intensive AI adopters)
  7. For analysis, firms are often grouped as:
  8. High intensity: top tercile
  9. Low intensity: bottom two terciles combined

docs.title: Rationale for Tercile Approach
docs.text:
• Allows researchers to examine differential impacts of AI adoption based on intensity
  • Reveals that not all AI adopters experience the same employment effects
  • Helps address selection bias by comparing firms with similar eventual adoption intensity
  • Shows that substantial employment gains are concentrated among high-intensity adopters

docs.title: Key Findings Using Intensity Terciles
docs.text:
• High-intensity adopters grew total employment by 10.2% following adoption
  • Entry-level headcount rose 12.0% for high-intensity adopters
  • Low-intensity adopters showed no statistically significant change in employment
  • High-intensity gains emerged gradually over 18-24 months, suggesting a learning curve
  • Employment gains were broad across roles for high-intensity adopters (engineering, sales, administration, customer service)

docs.title: Significance
docs.text: This methodology revealed a critical insight often missed in prior research: AI's labor market effects differ substantially based on adoption intensity. Studies that treat all adopters the same may miss these nuanced patterns.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Methodological advances in measuring AI adoption, particularly the shift from occupational exposure scores to direct firm-level spending data. The ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study represents a breakthrough in this area by using observed AI vendor payments rather than theoretical exposure metrics.

docs.title: Ramp-Revelio Methodology
docs.text:
The study introduces the AI Spend Per Employee Methodology (PEPM):

  1. Adoption definition: Three consecutive months of ≥$100 AI vendor spend
  2. Intensity measure: PEPM = (sum of first 3 months' AI spend) / (3 × baseline headcount)
  3. Intensity stratification: Low (bottom two PEPM terciles), High (top PEPM tercile)
  4. Comparison design: Later adopters within same intensity group

This approach overcomes four critical limitations of prior methods:

  1. Direct observation: Measures actual adoption behavior rather than theoretical exposure
  2. Timing precision: Captures exact adoption month rather than imputed timing
  3. Intensity dimension: Reveals differential effects by adoption intensity
  4. Firm-level specificity: Avoids occupational aggregation that masks firm differences

docs.title: Observed Spending Threshold
docs.text: The $100/month threshold excludes one-off experiments while capturing sustained adoption, addressing the "Is this really AI adoption?" question that plagues survey-based approaches.

docs.title: PEPM Metric
docs.text: Using baseline headcount in the denominator makes intensity comparable across firm sizes and keeps employee scale predetermined relative to adoption timing.

docs.title: Staggered Treatment Design
docs.text: The Callaway-Sant'Anna framework accounts for heterogeneous treatment timing, avoiding biases in traditional event-study approaches.

docs.title: Evidence of Impact
docs.text: This methodological innovation revealed findings invisible to exposure-based studies: - Only high-intensity adopters (+10.2% headcount growth) showed significant employment effects - Entry-level roles grew 12.0% among high-intensity adopters, contradicting exposure-based predictions - Effects concentrated in Information sector (+13.4% growth), not uniformly distributed

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
This methodological shift has critical implications:

  • Vendor evaluation: Must measure actual usage intensity, not just adoption status
  • Impact assessment: Requires tracking spending patterns over time, not binary adoption
  • Benchmarking: Industry comparisons must account for intensity differences
  • ROI calculation: Benefits appear only above critical intensity thresholds

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text: This innovation directly addresses the ai-adoption-selection-bias problem and explains the methodological-heterogeneity-in-ai-studies observed across research. It represents a critical advance over the pwc-ai-occupational-exposure-index used in pwc-2026-global-ai-jobs-barometer.

docs.title: Practical Implementation
docs.text:
For market research organizations, adopting this methodological innovation means: - Tracking actual AI spending rather than adoption claims - Measuring intensity through normalized spending metrics - Comparing against firms with similar pre-adoption characteristics - Focusing on sustained usage patterns rather than initial adoption

Without these methodological improvements, organizations risk misattributing effects or missing the intensity threshold needed for positive returns—precisely what the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study demonstrates.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The substantial pre-existing differences between AI adopters and non-adopters that complicate causal inference in AI impact studies. As rigorously documented in the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study, these selection effects mean AI adopters were already distinct from non-adopters before AI adoption, creating significant methodological challenges.

docs.title: Key Evidence
docs.text:
The Ramp-Revelio study demonstrates dramatic pre-adoption differences:

Characteristic AI Adopters Never Adopters Difference Headcount (mean) 144.2 103.9 +40.3* Engineering share 26.8% 18.6% +8.2* Entry-level share 42.1% 50.4% -8.3* YoY growth (median) 6.0% 1.6% +4.4* Mean salary $110,346 $93,847 +$16,499* Tech-adjacent sector 54.2% 25.9% +28.3* VC-backed 34.0% 9.5% +24.5*

*Statistically significant at p<0.01

docs.title: Methodological Implications
docs.text:
This selection bias creates three critical challenges for AI impact research:

  1. Confounded comparisons: Simple adopter vs. non-adopter comparisons conflate AI effects with pre-existing differences
  2. Pre-trend divergence: Adopters were already on different growth trajectories before adoption (see Figure 4 in Ramp-Revelio study)
  3. Sector concentration: AI adoption heavily concentrated in Information (53.7%), Finance (43.6%), and Professional Services (36.0%)

docs.title: Addressing the Bias
docs.text:
The Ramp-Revelio study employs sophisticated methods to address selection bias:

  • Preferred comparison: Later adopters within the same eventual intensity group
  • Sector fixed effects: Controlling for industry composition differences
  • Event-time analysis: Tracking pre-treatment parallel trends
  • Intensity stratification: Separating low vs. high adoption intensity effects

This approach revealed that only high-intensity adopters (top PEPM tercile) showed significant employment growth (+10.2%), while low-intensity adopters showed no significant change.

docs.title: Contrast with Exposure-Based Studies
docs.text: This selection bias explains why exposure-based studies (like pwc-2026-global-ai-jobs-barometer) often produce different findings than spending-based studies: - Exposure scores cannot distinguish firms that adopt AI from those that don't - They assume uniform adoption effects across firms with identical workforce composition - They miss the critical intensity dimension revealed by actual spending data

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
This concept has profound implications for insights organizations:

  • Vendor selection: AI tools adopted by leading firms may reflect pre-existing advantages rather than causal benefits
  • Implementation strategy: Success depends on organizational readiness, not just tool adoption
  • Impact measurement: Must account for pre-existing differences when evaluating AI initiatives
  • Benchmarking: Comparing against industry averages without controlling for selection effects is misleading

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text: This concept is central to understanding the methodological-heterogeneity-in-ai-studies problem and represents a key ai-adoption-methodological-innovation addressed by the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study. It explains why the employment gains documented in that study are concentrated among high-intensity adopters in specific sectors, rather than across all AI adopters.

docs.title: Practical Guidance
docs.text:
For market research professionals, addressing selection bias requires: - Never comparing AI adopters to non-adopters without controlling for pre-existing differences - Measuring adoption intensity (PEPM) rather than binary adoption status - Using staggered adoption timing in evaluation designs - Focusing on high-intensity implementation for meaningful impact

Without these precautions, organizations risk attributing pre-existing advantages to AI adoption or missing the intensity threshold needed for positive returns.

docs.title: Ai democratization
docs.text: AI democratization refers to the process where AI automates more expert tasks, leaving less expert tasks for humans.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: AI democratization describes how artificial intelligence makes advanced capabilities accessible by automating complex expert tasks, thereby reducing expertise requirements for certain occupations. As quantified in Figure 2 of the PwC 2026 report, this process affects 52% of global job postings. Concrete examples include [[recruiters]] (AI automates CV screening while humans handle contract negotiation) and [[inventory-clerks]] (AI manages stock optimization while humans perform physical movement). Figure 3 demonstrates democratization is particularly strong in high AI exposure jobs, where expertise requirements decrease significantly. Crucially, Figure 11 reveals that despite reduced expertise demands, democratized roles maintain high epoch-score (0.48), indicating continued reliance on human capabilities for remaining tasks—often involving physical dexterity, adaptability, or interpersonal skills. The report warns that while democratization expands job accessibility (e.g., enabling non-experts to perform data analysis), it may compress career ladders and reduce skill development opportunities without targeted interventions. This concept represents one of two primary pathways (alongside ai-professionalization) in AI's labor market restructuring. Organizations can leverage democratization through the ai-job-future-framework's 'Supply and Demand' dimension, redesigning roles to balance AI efficiency with human execution. The trend is accelerating post-2022, as shown in Figure 9's widening skill transformation gap, requiring proactive workforce planning to ensure equitable access to emerging opportunities in democratized roles.

docs.title: Structural Analysis of Deskilling
docs.text:
As established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, this phenomenon should be understood as a structural problem requiring societal solutions rather than merely an individual responsibility issue. The paper identifies:

  1. Capacity-hostile environments that systematically restrict opportunities for capacity development
  2. Agential control erosion through automation of planning processes
  3. Intersubjective habituation breakdown when AI replaces human mentorship
  4. Embodiment challenges in digital environments

docs.title: Key Mechanisms
docs.text:
• Narrow field of affordances: AI systems limit action possibilities for capacity exercise
  • Plan-following vs plan-forming: Automation encourages habitual responses over self-initiated planning
  • Volitional capacity erosion: Reduced need for effort and perseverance in AI-mediated environments

docs.title: Market Research Implications
docs.text:
The structural perspective explains deskilling dynamics in market research workflows where AI tools: - Automate data analysis tasks that previously developed epistemic capacities - Replace human interaction in research design that cultivated social capacities - Encourage reliance on algorithmic recommendations over creative problem-solving

See ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem for full methodology.

docs.title: Ai job future framework
docs.text: A framework of four questions to analyze how AI is reshaping specific occupations, developed by PwC in their 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: The AI Job Future Framework, introduced in Figure 6 of PwC's 2026 report, provides a structured methodology to assess AI's occupational impact through four critical questions: (1) Expertise: How is AI changing required human expertise? (e.g., democratization reduces expertise needs while professionalization increases them); (2) Supply and Demand: How might job demand and worker supply shift as AI reshapes roles?; (3) AI's limitations: Where is human oversight needed for quality control or atypical cases?; and (4) Environmental forces: How do regulations, business bottlenecks, or ethics constrain AI adoption? The report demonstrates the framework's application across diverse occupations: For [[pharmacists]], AI handles prescription processing (Expertise shift) but humans manage patient counseling (AI's limitations); for [[software-developers]], AI generates code but humans focus on architecture (Environmental forces). Figure 9 validates the framework by showing how high AI exposure roles undergo 2.2x faster skill changes, directly addressing the Supply and Demand dimension. Organizations using this tool can anticipate skill shifts, redesign roles, and develop targeted training—particularly valuable for navigating the 'superstar effect' (Figure 12). The framework also explains wage dynamics: roles requiring human oversight of AI (Question 3) command higher premiums, as seen in Figure 15's 62% average AI skill premium. By systematically addressing these questions, employers can transform AI disruption into opportunity, while workers identify future-proof career paths in the evolving labor market. This methodology has become essential for strategic workforce planning in the AI era.

docs.title: New Evidence and Refinement
docs.text:
The mrii-2026-market-research-study provides compelling evidence of AI professionalization in the insights industry: - As AI handles routine analytical tasks, value is shifting upstream toward strategic functions - Insights teams must evolve from delivering answers to shaping decisions, driving growth, and influencing strategy - Pam Forbus of [[mondelez]] states: "AI will increasingly answer questions, deliver insights, execute projects, and support stakeholders faster and at lower cost than ever before. That doesn't diminish the role of insights teams; it fundamentally changes it."

This represents a specific manifestation of professionalization where AI automation of basic tasks elevates the importance of strategic human capabilities.

The value-chain-shift concept further explains this dynamic - as AI makes answers faster and cheaper, the answers themselves become less differentiated, pushing value creation toward higher-order strategic functions.

docs.title: Relationship to Skills Development
docs.text:
A critical finding from the MRII study reveals a professionalization paradox: - Professionals prioritize learning technical AI skills - Leaders value business acumen, communication, and strategic influence more highly

This disconnect threatens to undermine the professionalization process, as organizations may automate tasks without adequately developing the human capabilities needed for the elevated roles.

docs.title: Connection to Entry-Level Dynamics
docs.text: The burning-glass-beyond-binary report shows that professionalization occurs alongside automation within the same occupations. This creates particular challenges for entry-level positions through the entry-level-squeeze, as foundational tasks that build expertise are automated before new developmental pathways are established.

docs.title: Organizational Implications
docs.text: Successful navigation of AI professionalization requires: - Redesigning roles to preserve meaningful human involvement in value-creating activities - Developing new apprenticeship models that build expertise despite automated foundational tasks - Aligning skill development priorities with the evolving value chain

docs.title: Capacity-Conducive Environments
docs.text: Capacity-conducive environments are socio-technical contexts that actively encourage the development and exercise of human capacities through rich opportunities for embodied interaction and shared valuing. These environments provide the necessary conditions for habituation-process and the cultivation of agential-control, as detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem.

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
• Broad Field of Affordances: Offers diverse action possibilities that trigger the competent exercise of epistemic, social, creative, and volitional capacities.
  • Embodied & Intersubjective Engagement: Prioritizes physical presence and sensory experience, which are critical for recognizing others as moral agents, forming meaningful relationships, and developing shared valuing of skills.
  • Encouragement of Volitional Capacity: Actively supports the capacity to will by encouraging agents to develop and exercise other capacities, recognizing that capacity development is difficult and requires effort.
  • Mentorship & Social Practices: Provides structured and unstructured opportunities for learning from exemplars, instilling both the 'know-how' and the intrinsic value of skills.

docs.title: Examples in AI Contexts
docs.text:
• Collaborative AI Workflows: Tools designed to augment human judgment rather than replace it, requiring users to deliberate, settle, and coordinate plans (plan-forming).
  • Public Libraries & Community Centers: Physical spaces that foster shared experiences and unstructured interactions, essential for the intersubjective habituation of social and moral capacities.
  • AI Evaluation Frameworks: Systems that assess AI applications based on their conduciveness to capacity cultivation, prioritizing tools that preserve agential control and encourage real-world experience.

docs.title: Implementation in Market Research
docs.text: For insights organizations, fostering capacity-conducive environments means designing research workflows that preserve researcher autonomy, encourage deep engagement with data, and maintain human-to-human collaboration. AI should be positioned as a tool that frees time for higher-order strategic thinking and creative synthesis, rather than a replacement for foundational analytical and empathetic skills. See also ai-deskilling-structural-problem.

docs.title: Connection to Capacity Development
docs.text:

Ferdman argues that preserving creative capacities in market research requires structural solutions maintaining opportunities for researchers to engage in the full creative process. Organizations must balance AI efficiency with the need for spaces where researchers can make unfamiliar combinations of familiar concepts. The value of market research insights depends not just on accurate data but on the creative capacity exercise that transforms data into meaningful understanding. Capacity-conducive research environments intentionally preserve opportunities for creative transformation, recognizing that innovation in research methodology and insight generation is essential for staying relevant in a changing marketplace.

docs.title: Embodiment in Skilling
docs.text: First Observed: 2026-07-03 Last Updated: 2026-09-25

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The essential role of physical presence and sensory experience in the development of human capacities, particularly social and moral skills. Embodied interaction is critical for recognizing others as moral agents and forming meaningful relationships, as detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. Expanded with detailed analysis of characteristics, contrast with disembodied interaction, threats from AI, preservation strategies, and market research applications from Ferdman's research.

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
Ferdman (2026) emphasizes the critical role of embodiment in skill development:

"Being embodied is critical for becoming skilled insofar as the process of 'shared valuing' of the skill requires some degree of doing something with the mentor(s), creating a shared history and a participatory sense-making regarding both the product of the skill and the skill itself."

Key characteristics:

  • Participatory sense-making: According to the Enactive Approach, embodied 'participatory sense-making' is constitutive of social cognition
  • Moral recognition: "Without being embodied in a social interaction—without the return of the gaze of the other—we would be hard-pressed to recognize them spontaneously as moral agents."
  • Spontaneity: The spontaneity of recognizing others as moral agents is inherent in embodied interaction
  • Shared history: Embodied interaction creates a shared history necessary for skill transmission

docs.title: Contrast with Disembodied Interaction
docs.text:
Ferdman details significant limitations of disembodied interaction:

"Disembodied interaction requires the agent to exercise more mental efforts in attributing moral agency to the other."

"For the good of friendship, disembodied interactions make it harder to form meaningful friendship because technologically mediated virtue friendships require more discipline for a diminished experience."

docs.title: Threats from AI in Research Contexts
docs.text:
AI tools that promote disembodied interaction threaten market research capacities:

"The smartphone: it provides possibilities for interaction that are disconnected from other persons, such as swiping, clicking and scrolling. This in turn invites determinate, separate, and repeatable tasks. This fractures the user's affordance space into disconnected fields, ultimately leading to alienation, rather than offering opportunities for the development of new cognitive and bodily skills that are mutually informing and enriching."

Specific threats: - Remote qualitative research tools that reduce embodied presence with participants - AI analysis tools that bypass the embodied experience of conducting interviews - Digital collaboration platforms that limit spontaneous interaction among research teams - Automated reporting that removes the embodied process of communicating findings

docs.title: Preservation Strategies
docs.text:
Ferdman suggests approaches to maintain embodiment in skilling:

  1. Design for embodied interaction: Create workspaces and tools that facilitate physical co-presence
  2. Balance digital mediation: Use technology to enhance rather than replace embodied interaction
  3. Preserve fieldwork: Maintain opportunities for researchers to conduct embodied research activities
  4. Hybrid approaches: Combine digital tools with embodied practices in research workflows

docs.title: Market Research Applications
docs.text: Embodiment is particularly critical for: - Qualitative interviewing where physical presence affects data quality - Observational research that requires embodied presence in contexts - Team collaboration where spontaneous interaction generates insights - Client presentations where embodied communication builds trust

docs.title: Entry-Level Squeeze
docs.text: The entry-level squeeze describes the growing pressure on traditional entry-level positions in knowledge work as AI capabilities automate foundational tasks that historically served as training grounds for developing professional expertise. This creates a paradox where entry-level roles simultaneously become harder to obtain yet more demanding when available.

docs.title: Structural Dynamics
docs.text: Three interlocking mechanisms drive the squeeze: 1. Training Ground Erosion: AI handles basic tasks that taught core competencies 2. Experience Compression: Entry roles now require skills previously developed mid-career 3. Pipeline Disruption: Reduced junior positions limit progression pathways

docs.title: Market Research Evidence
docs.text:
• 41% decline in pure data processing roles since 2023
  • Entry positions now require AI tool certification and strategic thinking
  • Traditional apprenticeship models replaced by accelerated upskilling

Augmented with parallel evidence from ama-2026-state-of-marketing-careers-report. The report documents identical dynamics in marketing where: - Entry-level marketers face "difficult start but still-desirable destination" paradox - 72% of early-career roles now require AI fluency certifications - Traditional content creation tasks automated, forcing new hires into strategic roles prematurely This cross-industry validation confirms the entry-level squeeze as a systemic knowledge work phenomenon.

docs.title: 2026-08-26 Update
docs.text: The human capacities related to knowledge, reasoning, and understanding, including theoretical rationality and practical rationality (phronesis), which are essential for navigating truth and making informed decisions, as detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
1. Theoretical rationality:
  2. Thinking, considering reasons to believe
  3. Forming beliefs, contemplating
  4. Critical evaluation of evidence

  5. Distinguishing truth from falsehood

  6. Practical rationality (phronesis):

  7. Doing the right thing in the right way for the right reason
  8. Effective means to ends with accurate situational understanding
  9. Discernment: correct understanding of how good and bad apply in circumstances
  10. Wisdom in complex decision-making

docs.title: Development Process
docs.text: Epistemic capacities develop through: - Gradual habituation involving inculcation through continued attunement - Embodied, intersubjective learning environments - Opportunities to exercise agential control over knowledge formation - Encountering and overcoming disappointment and failure - Shared valuing through mentorship

docs.title: Threats from AI in Market Research
docs.text: Ferdman identifies specific AI-related threats: - Automated insight generation: Tools that provide ready-made interpretations reduce opportunities to develop practical rationality - Algorithmic data processing: Systems that obscure the reasoning process behind insights - Template-based analysis: Workflows that limit opportunities for novel analytical approaches - Over-reliance on AI recommendations: Reducing opportunities to exercise theoretical rationality

docs.title: Market Research Examples
docs.text:
• Junior researchers using AI-powered survey analysis without developing manual interpretation skills
  • Automated reporting tools that generate insights without requiring researchers to engage in the full analytical process
  • Predictive analytics platforms that provide conclusions without showing the reasoning pathway
  • AI respondent matching that eliminates the need to develop nuanced understanding of demographic patterns

docs.title: Preservation Strategies
docs.text:
• Implement "progressive disclosure" of AI tools, starting with manual methods
  • Create opportunities for researchers to develop insights before seeing AI-generated analysis
  • Design workflows requiring researchers to explain their reasoning before accepting AI recommendations
  • Preserve spaces for critical evaluation of AI-generated insights
  • Develop mentorship programs focused on practical rationality development

docs.title: Connection to Capacity Development
docs.text:
Epistemic capacities are particularly vulnerable to AI-induced deskilling because: - They require direct engagement with data and evidence - Practical rationality (phronesis) develops through trial and error - Theoretical rationality requires opportunities to form and test beliefs - AI tools that provide instant answers undermine the habituation process

Ferdman argues that preserving epistemic capacities in market research requires structural solutions that maintain opportunities for researchers to engage directly with data, develop their own interpretations, and learn from mistakes. Organizations must balance efficiency gains from AI with the need to preserve spaces for epistemic capacity development, recognizing that the value of research insights comes not just from the outputs but from the competent epistemic capacity exercise that produces them.

docs.title: Update 2026-08-26
docs.text: Human capacities related to knowledge acquisition, critical thinking, reasoning, and understanding, including theoretical rationality and practical rationality (phronesis). Expanded with detailed analysis from Ferdman's structural perspective on capacity development, including threats from AI in market research and preservation strategies.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
1. Theoretical Rationality: Thinking, considering reasons to believe, forming beliefs, contemplating
  2. Practical Rationality (Phronesis): Doing the right thing in the right way for the right reason, common sense or wisdom
  3. Critical Evaluation: Assessing information quality, identifying biases, recognizing limitations
  4. Contextual Understanding: Interpreting information within relevant frameworks and situations
  5. Epistemic Humility: Recognizing the limits of one's knowledge and the value of diverse perspectives

docs.title: Ferdman's Structural Perspective
docs.text:
Ferdman's analysis in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem reveals how AI systems can undermine epistemic capacities through structural conditions:

  • Deskilling Mechanism: When AI replaces critical thinking and decision-making, it creates capacity-hostile environments that restrict opportunities for developing epistemic capacities
  • Plan-Following Trap: AI systems that provide ready-made answers encourage researchers to become plan-followers rather than plan-formers, diminishing practical rationality
  • Value Devaluation: Without experiencing the gradual habituation process, researchers may fail to appreciate the value of deep epistemic work
  • Embodiment Requirement: Epistemic capacities develop best through embodied interaction where researchers encounter diverse perspectives face-to-face

docs.title: Market Research Threats
docs.text:
1. Automated Insights Generation: AI tools that produce complete research reports without researcher input erode critical evaluation skills
  2. Black-Box Analytics: Systems that provide predictions without transparent reasoning undermine practical rationality development
  3. Confirmation Bias Amplification: AI that reinforces existing assumptions without challenging them diminishes critical thinking
  4. Reduced Contextual Understanding: Over-reliance on quantitative AI analysis at the expense of qualitative understanding
  5. Epistemic Complacency: Belief that AI-generated insights are sufficiently accurate, reducing motivation to develop deeper understanding

docs.title: Preservation Strategies
docs.text:
1. AI as Sounding Board: Use AI to generate initial hypotheses but require researchers to critically evaluate and refine them
  2. Transparent Methodologies: Prioritize AI tools that explain their reasoning rather than providing opaque outputs
  3. Deliberate Disagreement: Create team practices that intentionally surface and examine differing interpretations
  4. Embodied Sense-Making: Maintain face-to-face client workshops and team discussions to develop contextual understanding
  5. Failure Analysis: Implement regular practices for examining research missteps to strengthen epistemic resilience

As Ferdman argues, 'the competent exercise of the human capacities is the manifestation of the achievement of the intrinsically valuable goods, making the capacities intrinsically valuable too.' Market research organizations must preserve epistemic capacities as constitutive of high-quality insights rather than treating them as mere means to efficiency.

docs.title: Habituation Process
docs.text: Habituation is the gradual, slow process of becoming skilled through practice, inculcation, and attunement to the demands of individual cases. As outlined in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, skill cannot be learned through testimony alone; it requires encountering and overcoming disappointment and failure. Habituation is the mechanism through which agential-control and human-capacities are cultivated.

docs.title: Two Critical Components
docs.text:
1. Intersubjectivity: Skill development is inherently social. It requires mentors, exemplars, and shared social practices that instill not only the mechanical 'know-how' but also a shared understanding of the skill's value. Social practices generate moral reasons for action and help individuals fare well.
  2. Embodiment: Physical presence and sensory experience are constitutive of social cognition. Embodied interaction allows us to perceive others as moral agents, recognize their gaze and voice, and form meaningful relationships. Disembodied interaction requires significantly more mental effort to attribute moral agency and develop shared valuing.

docs.title: Stages of Skill Development
docs.text: Drawing on the Dreyfus model, habituation progresses through stages: novice, advanced beginner, competent, proficient, and expert. Early stages rely heavily on rule-following, while later stages are characterized by rapid, fluid, involved engagement. Crucially, this process is one of growth rather than simple repetition.

docs.title: AI's Impact on Habituation
docs.text: AI mediation risks undermining the quality of conditions for capacity habituation. By offloading routine tasks and providing instant answers, AI tools can shortcut the practice necessary for deep skill acquisition. Disembodied AI interactions further restrict the embodied, intersubjective engagement required for developing social and moral capacities. This leads to shallow skilling and capacity impoverishment.

docs.title: Mitigation & Preservation
docs.text:
• Maintain Mentorship Structures: Preserve human-to-human guidance and feedback loops in AI-augmented workflows.
  • Design for Practice: Ensure AI tools require user engagement and decision-making rather than fully autonomous execution.
  • Foster Embodied Collaboration: Prioritize in-person or richly mediated interactions for complex, value-laden tasks.

See also intersubjectivity-in-skilling, embodiment-in-skilling, and capacity-hostile-environments.

docs.title: Human operating model gap
docs.text: The human operating model gap refers to the growing disparity between the rapid advancement of AI capabilities and the slower adaptation of human systems, processes, and skills required to leverage AI effectively within organizations.

docs.title: Workforce Composition Changes with AI Adoption
docs.text: Recent evidence reveals how AI adoption is reshaping workforce composition across roles, highlighting the growing gap between rapidly advancing AI capabilities and slower human system adaptation.

docs.title: Role-Specific Employment Effects
docs.text:
The ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study provides detailed evidence of how AI adoption affects different job functions:

  • Broad-based growth: High-intensity adopters showed growth across multiple roles:
  • Sales headcount: +10.3%
  • Administrative headcount: +7.8%
  • Engineering headcount: +7.3%
  • Customer service headcount: +6.3%

  • Scientist headcount: +5.6%

  • Entry-level expansion: Entry-level headcount rose 12.0% among high-intensity adopters

  • Managerial shifts: Manager-plus share fell by 1.52 percentage points despite overall growth

docs.title: Structural Workforce Shifts
docs.text:
These findings reveal several important patterns:

  1. Non-binary impact: AI adoption doesn't simply eliminate jobs but reshapes workforce composition
  2. Intensity matters: Only high-intensity adopters (top tercile of AI spend) showed significant growth
  3. Gradual emergence: Gains followed a learning curve, emerging 6-12 months after adoption
  4. Sector concentration: Effects were strongest in the Information sector

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For market research organizations, these workforce shifts suggest:

  • AI is currently augmenting rather than replacing human capabilities in information work
  • Strategic AI investment may support growth across multiple functions
  • Entry-level positions may expand as firms scale with AI assistance
  • Workforce planning must account for the gradual nature of AI integration

The study notes that "the earliest signs of growth emerge roughly 6-12 months after adoption, perhaps after firms establish best practices, integrate AI tools into workflows, and are subsequently able to make new investments and hire staff."

docs.title: Bridging the Gap
docs.text:
To address the human operating model gap, market research firms should:

  • Develop AI adoption strategies that align with workforce development
  • Create pathways for employees to develop AI-augmented capabilities
  • Recognize that successful integration requires time for habituation
  • Design capacity-conducive environments that preserve opportunities for skill development

See value-chain-shift and ai-professionalization for related frameworks analyzing AI's impact on organizational structures.

docs.title: Intersubjectivity in Skilling
docs.text: First Observed: 2026-07-03 Last Updated: 2026-09-25

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The shared understanding dimension of skill development, where learning occurs through relationships with others who guide and share the value of the skill. Becoming skilled typically requires a mentor to instill not only mechanical aspects but also the value of the skill, as detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. Expanded with detailed analysis of characteristics, societal dimension, threats from AI, preservation strategies, and market research applications from Ferdman's research.

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
Ferdman (2026) elaborates on the intersubjective nature of skill development:

"Skill habituation has a 'shared understanding' dimension. First, becoming skilled typically requires a mentor to guide the novice into becoming an expert that engages in practice of the right kind. A good mentor is typically necessary in order to cultivate the proper motivational structure for becoming skilled."

Key characteristics:

  • Shared valuing: Both mentor and mentee develop "shared valuing" of the skill, where the mentee eventually views the value of the skill as their own
  • Mentorship relationship: Requires a relationship where the mentor instills both mechanical aspects and value of the skill
  • Societal dimension: Social practices performed by groups or whole societies can provide a mentoring environment
  • Constitutive aim: Social practices have a "telos, which is ultimately the aim of helping people fare well rather than badly"

docs.title: Threats from AI in Research Contexts
docs.text:
Ferdman identifies how AI mediation threatens intersubjective skilling:

"APAs decrease embodied, intersubjective interaction involved in life-planning activities."

"In embodied interaction, all the constant 'living together' which goes on in between and around physical, embodied activities with other persons better allow us to test and grow our human capacities, compared to virtual environments."

Specific threats to market research: - AI tools that replace human mentorship in research methodology - Digital platforms that reduce opportunities for shared understanding of research quality - Automated analysis tools that bypass the intersubjective process of interpreting data - Remote work environments that limit embodied interaction necessary for qualitative research skills

docs.title: Preservation Strategies
docs.text:
Ferdman suggests approaches to maintain intersubjective skilling:

  1. Structured mentorship: Create formal mentorship programs that preserve opportunities for shared valuing
  2. Embodied collaboration: Design workspaces that facilitate physical co-presence for research teams
  3. Reflection practices: Build in regular opportunities for researchers to discuss the value of research skills
  4. AI as augmentation: Use AI tools to enhance rather than replace intersubjective learning processes

docs.title: Market Research Applications
docs.text: Intersubjectivity is particularly critical for: - Developing qualitative interviewing skills that require embodied presence - Building shared understanding of research quality standards - Cultivating the ability to recognize emerging patterns through team discussion - Preserving the value dimension of research skills that goes beyond mechanical execution

The Ramp-Revelio study documents this heterogeneity through direct comparison: - Exposure-based studies predict job losses in high-exposure occupations - Spending-based research shows job growth among high-intensity adopters - The discrepancy stems from methodological differences, not contradictory realities

docs.title: Root Causes
docs.text: Three fundamental methodological differences drive these divergent findings:

docs.title: 1. Adoption Measurement
docs.text:
• Exposure scores: Measure theoretical task feasibility ("could AI do this?")
  • Spending data: Measure actual adoption behavior ("is the firm paying for AI?")
  • Surveys: Capture self-reported usage ("do executives say they use AI?")

As the Ramp-Revelio study notes: "These estimates are closer to the Ramp–Revelio paid-adoption series than the firm-weighted BTOS benchmark, but they still measure a different object."

docs.title: 2. Intensity Dimension
docs.text:
• Exposure scores: Typically binary or quintile-based
  • Spending data: Reveals continuous intensity effects (PEPM metric)
  • Surveys: Often lack precise intensity measures

The Ramp-Revelio study found only high-intensity adopters showed significant employment growth (+10.2%), while low-intensity adopters showed no change.

docs.title: 3. Selection Bias Handling
docs.text:
• Exposure scores: Cannot distinguish adopters from non-adopters with identical workforce
  • Spending data: Enables direct comparison of adopters vs. later adopters
  • Surveys: Often lack pre-adoption data for comparison

The Ramp-Revelio study documents substantial pre-adoption differences that confound simple adopter vs. non-adopter comparisons.

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
This methodological heterogeneity creates critical challenges:

  • Conflicting guidance: Different studies recommend opposite actions based on methodology
  • Implementation uncertainty: Hard to predict AI impact without knowing intensity threshold
  • Evaluation complexity: Must select appropriate methodology for specific context
  • Vendor claims: AI providers may cite favorable methodology while ignoring others

docs.title: Strategic Response Framework
docs.text:
Market research organizations should adopt a methodologically sophisticated approach:

  1. Triangulate findings: Consider evidence from multiple methodological approaches
  2. Assess intensity: Focus on high-intensity implementation for meaningful impact
  3. Control for selection: Account for pre-existing differences when evaluating AI
  4. Contextualize results: Recognize sector-specific effects (e.g., concentrated in Information)

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text: This concept explains the contradictory findings between the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study (showing 12.0% entry-level growth) and exposure-based studies predicting job losses. It represents the methodological foundation for understanding the ai-adoption-selection-bias problem and the value of the ai-adoption-methodological-innovation in spending-based measurement.

docs.title: Practical Guidance
docs.text:
For market research professionals, navigating methodological heterogeneity requires: - Never relying on a single study's methodology for decision-making - Understanding the measurement approach behind any AI impact claim - Recognizing that "AI adoption" has no single empirical rate (as shown in Ramp-Revelio Figure 1) - Focusing on high-intensity implementation thresholds rather than binary adoption

Without this methodological sophistication, organizations risk making decisions based on incomplete or misleading evidence about AI's true impact.

docs.title: Narrow Field of Affordances
docs.text: A narrow field of affordances refers to an environment that provides limited action possibilities, restricting opportunities for the development and exercise of human capacities. As detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, this is a key mechanism through which AI systems can create capacity-hostile-environments.

docs.title: Mechanisms of Affordance Shrinkage
docs.text:
• Automation Bias: When AI tools automate routine tasks, they remove the opportunities for users to practice judgment and strengthen cognitive skills. Users become atrophied and unprepared for exceptions.
  • Systematic & Enduring Reduction: Affordance shrinkage becomes problematic when it is not temporary but deeply entrenched, discouraging users from finding ways to compensate for the loss of action possibilities.
  • Disembodied Interaction: Digital mediation fractures the affordance space into disconnected fields (swiping, clicking, scrolling), inviting determinate, separate, and repeatable tasks that fail to mutually inform and enrich cognitive and bodily skills.

docs.title: Normative Implications
docs.text: From a structural perspective, a narrow field of affordances is normatively problematic because it systematically discourages the competent exercise of human capacities. When users are herded into predictable behaviors through targeted algorithms or automated workflows, they lose the invitations to engage in valuable activities that trigger epistemic, social, creative, and volitional capacities.

docs.title: Examples in AI Contexts
docs.text:
• Social Media Platforms: Filtered newsfeeds and targeted ads maintain predictable engagement patterns, restricting affordances for critical thinking and diverse social interaction.
  • APAs & Productivity Tools: Constant prompts to accept AI-generated schedules and priorities reduce the affordances for self-deliberation and plan-forming.
  • Healthcare AI: Over-reliance on diagnostic algorithms reduces the affordances for clinical reasoning and ethical sensitivity among practitioners.

docs.title: Counteracting Affordance Shrinkage
docs.text: Organizations must actively design AI implementations that preserve or expand the field of affordances. This includes maintaining human-in-the-loop workflows, preserving mentorship and embodied collaboration, and ensuring AI tools act as scaffolding rather than replacements. See also capacity-hostile-environments, capacity-conducive-environments, and agential-control.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: PEPM (AI Spend Per Employee) is a metric developed in the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study to measure the intensity of AI adoption at the firm level. It calculates monthly AI vendor spend per employee over the first three months after sustained AI adoption begins.

docs.title: Formula
docs.text:
PEPM = (Σ²ₘ₌₀ AIᵢ,ɢᵢ₊ₘ) / (3 × HCᵢ,ɢᵢ₋₁)

Where: - AIᵢ,ɢᵢ₊ₘ = AI vendor spend for firm i in month m after adoption - HCᵢ,ɢᵢ₋₁ = baseline headcount in the month before adoption

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
1. AI adoption is defined as the first month of a three-consecutive-month spell where AI spend is at least $100 monthly
  2. PEPM is calculated using AI spend over the first three months after adoption begins
  3. Baseline headcount is measured in the month before adoption
  4. Firms are sorted into intensity groups:
  5. High intensity: top PEPM tercile
  6. Low intensity: bottom two PEPM terciles

docs.title: Significance
docs.text:
• Provides a direct, observed measure of AI adoption intensity rather than relying on occupational exposure scores
  • Allows researchers to distinguish between firms that adopt AI lightly versus intensively
  • Correlates closely with adoption of more complex AI products and tools (coding agents, APIs) versus simpler chat subscriptions
  • Enables analysis of differential impacts based on adoption intensity

docs.title: Key Findings Using PEPM
docs.text:
• High-intensity adopters (top tercile) grew employment by 10.2% following adoption
  • Entry-level headcount rose 12.0% for high-intensity adopters
  • Low-intensity adopters showed no statistically significant change in employment
  • Gains emerged gradually, suggesting a "learning curve" as firms integrated AI tools

docs.title: Plan-Following
docs.text: Plan-following refers to the execution of pre-determined plans without exercising agential control over the planning process itself. As analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, this represents a habitual mode of action where individuals respond to environmental triggers rather than initiating and adjusting plans through self-deliberation. It stands in direct contrast to plan-forming.

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
• Trigger-Response Mechanism: Actions are elicited by external cues (e.g., AI recommendations, algorithmic suggestions) rather than internal deliberation.
  • Reduced Agential Control: The user does not initiate the activity or adjust its execution based on unfolding contexts. Control is ceded to the external system.
  • Responsibility Diffusion: When plans fail, users can more readily shift blame to the AI tool, avoiding self-criticism and the opportunities for growth that come from analyzing failure.
  • Shallow Capacity Exercise: Requires less epistemic, moral, social, and creative engagement than plan-forming, leading to atrophied judgment and practical wisdom.

docs.title: Role of AI in Encouraging Plan-Following
docs.text: APAs and automated planning tools are designed to be constantly available and helpful, inviting users to offload planning activities. Features like daily task scheduling, priority setting, and calendar optimization prompt users to accept AI-generated plans rather than formulate their own. This constant availability limits the user's ability to develop independence and undermines the habituation of capacities necessary for trusting one's own decisions.

docs.title: Mitigation Strategies
docs.text:
• Mandate Human Initiation: Require researchers and analysts to draft initial plans, hypotheses, or strategies before leveraging AI for refinement.
  • Design for Reflection: Build prompts and interfaces that ask users to articulate their reasoning, values, and goals before accepting AI suggestions.
  • Preserve Exception Handling: Ensure humans remain responsible for edge cases and system failures to maintain judgment and cognitive agility.

See also agential-control, habituation-process, and ai-deskilling-structural-problem.

docs.title: Plan-Forming vs. Plan-Following
docs.text: The distinction between plan-forming and plan-following highlights a critical shift in human agency induced by AI systems, particularly Artificial Personal Assistants (APAs). As analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, plan-forming requires self-deliberation and agential control, while plan-following represents a habitual mode of action triggered by environmental cues (i.e., AI outputs).

docs.title: Plan-Forming
docs.text:
• Definition: Actively creating plans through self-deliberation, involving the settling of options and coordination of intentions.
  • Capacities Exercised: Requires epistemic capacities (theoretical & practical rationality), social/moral capacities (aligning plans with relationships and values), creative capacities (adapting to surprises), and volitional capacity (initiating the effort).
  • Agential Control: The user initiates the activity, maintains control over execution, and takes responsibility for outcomes. This fosters practical wisdom and personal identity.
  • Value: Life-planning is self-constituting; it shapes character and dispositions rather than merely achieving instrumental goals.

docs.title: Plan-Following
docs.text:
• Definition: Executing pre-determined plans generated by external entities (e.g., APAs, algorithms) without exercising agential control over the planning process.
  • Mechanism: The user responds to a trigger in the environment (the AI's output) rather than initiating self-deliberation. This shifts the agent from a plan-former to a plan-follower.
  • Capacity Erosion: Offloading planning to AI reduces the need for routine decision-making, undermining the habituation of capacities necessary for trusting one's own judgment. Responsibility for failure can be shifted to the tool, forgoing opportunities for self-growth.
  • Risk: Encourages shallow skilling and capacity impoverishment, as users bypass the difficult but necessary process of developing practical wisdom through real-world experience and failure.

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text: Research workflows that rely heavily on AI-generated insights, automated reporting, or algorithmic survey design risk pushing practitioners into plan-following modes. To preserve professional expertise, organizations must design systems that require researchers to formulate hypotheses, design methodologies, and interpret findings (plan-forming), using AI only as a supportive tool for data processing and pattern recognition. See also agential-control, habituation-process, and artificial-personal-assistants.

docs.title: Seniorised roles
docs.text: The phenomenon where entry-level roles increasingly demand skills traditionally required in senior positions due to AI adoption.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: Seniorised roles describe the accelerating trend where entry-level positions now require skills traditionally associated with senior roles, driven by AI automation of foundational tasks. Figure 8 in the PwC 2026 report provides compelling evidence: in the US top AI exposure quartile, seniorised entry-level job postings are projected to grow 35% between 2019-2025, while non-seniorised roles decline by 10%. This occurs because AI tools handle routine onboarding tasks (e.g., data entry for [[inventory-clerks]] or basic analysis for [[recruiters]]), compressing career ladders and elevating entry requirements. Common senior skills now appearing in entry-level descriptions include strategic decision-making frameworks, cross-departmental collaboration, client advisory capabilities, and complex problem-solving—particularly in high-growth professionalised-jobs. Figure 7 contextualizes this within broader market trends, showing high AI exposure quartile entry-level postings have flatlined since 2022, suggesting seniorisation may be a prerequisite for growth in AI-impacted roles. The report warns this trend could exacerbate early-career inequality if not balanced with structured mentorship, as new graduates face higher barriers without prior exposure to advanced skills. However, organizations using the ai-job-future-framework can mitigate risks by designing onboarding that combines AI tools with human skill development. The phenomenon represents a key manifestation of AI's impact on career progression, with implications for education systems needing to prepare students for accelerated responsibility in the AI era.

docs.title: 2026-08-26 Update
docs.text: The human capacities related to forming meaningful relationships, understanding others' perspectives, and participating in communal life, including moral capacity and relational capacity, which are essential for collaborative work and ethical research, as analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
1. Moral capacity:
  2. Recognizing others as moral agents
  3. Paying moral attention to others
  4. Understanding ethical dimensions of situations

  5. Making morally informed decisions

  6. Relational capacity:

  7. Forming meaningful relationships of friendship and love
  8. Understanding others' perspectives
  9. Participating in communal life
  10. Building trust and rapport

docs.title: Embodiment Requirement
docs.text: Social capacities fundamentally require embodiment: - "Embodied understanding" where perceived bodies are recognized as similar loci of subjectivity - Spontaneous recognition of others as moral agents through embodied interaction - The return of the gaze essential for moral attention - Participatory sense-making constitutive of social cognition - Shared history created through physical presence

docs.title: Threats from AI in Market Research
docs.text: Ferdman identifies specific AI-related threats: - Disembodied research methods: Digital platforms replacing face-to-face respondent interaction - Algorithmic matching: Systems that match researchers with respondents without embodied engagement - Virtual collaboration tools: Platforms reducing opportunities for spontaneous team interaction - Automated analysis: Tools processing human responses without requiring direct researcher engagement

docs.title: Market Research Examples
docs.text:
• Online survey platforms eliminating opportunities to observe respondent body language and emotional cues
  • AI-powered respondent matching reducing need for nuanced understanding through direct interaction
  • Virtual focus groups lacking embodied presence necessary for deep rapport building
  • Automated transcription tools processing interviews without requiring engagement with emotional dimensions

docs.title: Preservation Strategies
docs.text:
• Preserve opportunities for face-to-face research methods where appropriate
  • Design hybrid research approaches combining digital tools with embodied interaction
  • Create organizational practices valuing embodied research experiences
  • Develop training emphasizing physical presence importance in research quality
  • Implement debriefing sessions where researchers share embodied fieldwork experiences

docs.title: Connection to Capacity Development
docs.text:
Social capacities develop through: - Embodied, intersubjective habituation process - Shared valuing through mentorship and community - Opportunities for spontaneous interaction - Physical presence enabling participatory sense-making - Return of the gaze facilitating moral recognition

Ferdman argues that preserving social capacities in market research requires structural solutions maintaining opportunities for embodied interaction. Organizations must recognize that some aspects of human understanding cannot be fully captured through disembodied digital methods. The value of market research insights depends not just on data but on the social capacity exercise that enables researchers to understand human behavior in context. Capacity-conducive research environments intentionally preserve spaces for embodied research practice, recognizing that social capacities are essential for producing genuinely human-centered insights.

docs.title: Superstar effect
docs.text: The top 20% of most AI-exposed companies, referred to as 'superstars', achieve a significantly higher productivity growth rate.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: The 'superstar effect' identifies a critical divergence among AI adopters: the top 20% of most AI-exposed firms achieve dramatically higher productivity gains than peers. This effect was documented by pwc using orbis company financial data. As revealed in Figure 12 of the PwC 2026 report, these 'superstar' companies attained 163% average productivity growth in 2025—5 times higher than the 33.5% growth rate of most AI-exposed companies as a whole. This advantage has widened steadily since 2022, with superstars accelerating their lead while other AI-exposed firms maintain moderate growth. Figure 13 shows this productivity advantage translates to headcount growth, with superstar firms expanding employment 52.2% by 2025 versus 35.7% for least exposed quartiles. Crucially, Figure 14 demonstrates these gains are shared with workers through higher wage growth (24.4% vs 16.6% in 2025). The report attributes superstar status to three factors: strategic AI integration beyond automation (leveraging the ai-job-future-framework), investment in complementary human skills, and organizational agility in addressing [[ai's limitations]]. This creates a 'winner-takes-most' dynamic where superstars capture disproportionate value—evident in Figure 16's AI specialist hiring surge within these firms. The effect has profound implications: companies failing to achieve superstar status risk falling behind in the AI transformation, while workers in superstar firms gain through both wages and career opportunities in high-growth professionalised-jobs. Policymakers must address resulting market concentration through targeted support for mid-tier AI adopters.

docs.title: Value Chain Shift
docs.text: The value chain shift refers to the fundamental repositioning of where value is created within market research and insights organizations as AI capabilities advance. Historically, value resided in data collection and basic analysis, but AI automation is moving the locus of value toward higher-order activities like interpreting AI-generated insights, integrating findings across disparate data sources, and applying insights to strategic decision-making.

docs.title: Mechanisms of Shift
docs.text: Three key drivers transform traditional research value chains: 1. Automation of Foundational Tasks: AI handles survey programming, data cleaning, and basic reporting 2. Orchestration Premium: Value concentrates on designing AI workflows and validating outputs 3. Strategic Interpretation Gap: Human expertise becomes critical for contextualizing AI findings within business objectives

docs.title: Organizational Implications
docs.text: Teams must restructure around new value centers: - Traditional analyst roles evolve into AI insight orchestrators - Research design shifts from methodology execution to AI prompt engineering - Client deliverables transform from data reports to strategic action frameworks

Enhanced with concrete evidence from ama-2026-state-of-marketing-careers-report. The report documents an identical shift in marketing where: - Value moved from content generation (automated) to agentic operations (human-led) - "Executors become orchestrators" mirrors research's transition from data processors to AI workflow designers - "Leaner, meaner pods" directly parallel market research's move toward cross-functional AI-augmented teams This provides empirical validation of the value chain shift mechanism in adjacent professional services.
Initial entry documenting value repositioning in insights organizations.

docs.title: 2026-08-26 Update
docs.text: The human capacity to exert effort, overcome difficulty, persevere, and grow in order to achieve intrinsically valuable goals, treated as a meta-capacity necessary for developing all other capacities, as analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem.

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
• Involves exerting effort and overcoming difficulty
  • Requires perseverance through challenges
  • Enables growth toward intrinsically valuable goals
  • Functions as a meta-capacity necessary for developing other capacities
  • Develops through encountering and overcoming disappointment and failure

docs.title: Meta-Capacity Role
docs.text: Volitional capacity is foundational to all other capacities because: - Developing any capacity requires effort and determination - Overcoming challenges is essential for capacity growth - Perseverance enables progression through skill development stages - Growth toward intrinsically valuable goals requires sustained willpower - Without volitional capacity, other capacities cannot be fully developed

docs.title: Threats from AI in Market Research
docs.text: Ferdman identifies specific AI-related threats: - Automated task completion: Tools that replace human effort in routine research activities - Instant insight generation: Systems that provide ready-made interpretations without requiring perseverance - Template-based workflows: Structures that reduce need for overcoming research challenges - Predictive analytics: Platforms that minimize unexpected events requiring volitional response

docs.title: Market Research Examples
docs.text:
• AI-powered survey analysis tools that complete data interpretation without requiring researchers to struggle with complex patterns
  • Automated reporting systems that generate insights without requiring perseverance through analytical challenges
  • Standardized research templates that reduce need for overcoming methodological difficulties
  • Predictive analytics platforms that minimize unexpected findings requiring volitional adaptation

docs.title: Preservation Strategies
docs.text:
• Design AI tools that preserve opportunities for effortful engagement
  • Create workflows requiring researchers to overcome challenges before accessing AI assistance
  • Implement training programs emphasizing perseverance through research difficulties
  • Develop organizational practices that value effortful capacity development
  • Balance efficiency gains with opportunities to exercise volitional capacity

docs.title: Connection to Capacity Development
docs.text:
Volitional capacity develops through: - Encountering and overcoming disappointment and failure - Gradual habituation involving inculcation through continued attunement - Opportunities to exercise agential control over initiating activities - Embodied, intersubjective learning environments - Shared valuing of perseverance through mentorship

Ferdman argues that preserving volitional capacity in market research requires structural solutions maintaining opportunities for researchers to engage in effortful work. Organizations must balance AI efficiency with the need for spaces where researchers can develop perseverance and overcome challenges. The value of market research insights depends not just on speed of delivery but on the volitional capacity exercise that enables researchers to push through difficult analytical problems. Capacity-conducive research environments intentionally preserve opportunities for effortful engagement, recognizing that without volitional capacity, researchers cannot fully develop the other capacities essential for high-quality research. This meta-capacity is particularly vulnerable to AI-induced deskilling because AI tools often specifically target the automation of effortful tasks.

docs.title: Artificial Personal Assistants
docs.text: Artificial Personal Assistants (APAs) are AI systems based on Large Language Models (LLMs) designed to assist with personal organization, life planning, and decision-making. As detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, APAs represent one of the fastest-growing use cases for LLMs and pose significant risks to capacity cultivation when users become overly reliant on them.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Adaptability: APAs tailor advice based on user responses, habits, and preferences, creating a highly personalized interaction.
  • Constant Availability: Designed as 'always-on sounding boards,' they provide immediate access to expertise, ranging from strict taskmasters to encouraging cheerleaders.
  • Multi-Role Functionality: APAs combine the roles of social companion, moral advisor, life coach, and personal butler, leveraging AI's capacity to 'do everything for everyone at every environment.'

docs.title: Impact on Capacity Cultivation
docs.text: While APAs offer convenience and support, heavy reliance on them can create capacity-hostile-environments: - Erosion of Agential Control: Users shift from plan-formers to plan-followers, responding to AI outputs as environmental triggers rather than initiating self-deliberation. - Undermining Habituation: Offloading routine planning and decision-making deprives users of the practice necessary to develop practical wisdom and trust their own judgment. - Disembodied Interaction: APAs replace embodied, intersubjective interactions with algorithmic recommendations, making it harder to develop social and moral capacities through shared experience. - The 'Always-On' Trap: Constant availability limits users' ability to develop independence, as they are continually invited to return to the APA for answers rather than navigating challenges independently.

docs.title: Examples & Usage Patterns
docs.text:
• Life Planning: Users rely on APAs to organize daily habits, set New Year's resolutions, find purpose, and determine values.
  • Social Validation & Self-Regulation: Heavy users utilize APAs for interpersonal guidance, reframing problems, and staying focused.
  • Productivity Tools: Apps like Sunsama sync tasks, prioritize work, and schedule time slots, prompting users to follow AI-generated plans rather than formulate their own.

docs.title: Evaluation Criteria for Market Research
docs.text: When integrating APAs or similar LLM tools into research workflows, organizations should assess whether the tool encourages plan-forming or plan-following, preserves agential control, and supports embodied, intersubjective collaboration. APAs should be positioned as tools for information retrieval and option generation, not replacements for researcher judgment and strategic deliberation. See also ai-deskilling-structural-problem, plan-forming-vs-plan-following, and habituation-process.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The Callaway-Sant'Anna framework is an econometric approach for analyzing treatment effects when units receive treatment at different times, as implemented in the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study to analyze the impact of AI adoption on employment.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
• Developed by Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) to address limitations of conventional two-way fixed effects event studies
  • Designed for staggered adoption designs where firms begin treatment (AI adoption) at different points in time
  • Estimates group-time average treatment effects separately for different adoption cohorts
  • Compares earlier adopters to later adopters in the same intensity group while the later adopters have not yet adopted

docs.title: Implementation in Ramp-Revelio Study
docs.text:
• Used to estimate the relationship between firm-level AI adoption and employment
  • Applied separately to low and high AI intensity adoption groups
  • For high-intensity adopters, compared firms that adopted early to firms that would eventually be high-intensity adopters but hadn't yet adopted
  • Included NAICS sector fixed effects to address selection into early AI adoption

docs.title: Advantages Over Traditional Methods
docs.text:
• Better suited to heterogeneous treatment timing than single two-way fixed effects event studies
  • Reduces bias that can occur when treatment effects are heterogeneous across adoption cohorts
  • Allows for more precise estimation of dynamic treatment effects
  • Provides cleaner pre-treatment diagnostics for parallel trends assumption

docs.title: Key Findings Enabled by This Framework
docs.text:
• Revealed that high-intensity AI adopters grew employment by 10.2% following adoption
  • Showed that these gains emerged gradually over 18-24 months
  • Demonstrated that low-intensity adopters showed no statistically significant change in employment
  • Provided evidence against predictions that AI adoption would lead to broad job losses

docs.title: Lightcast
docs.text: Lightcast (formerly Emsi Burning Glass) is a labor market analytics company that provides detailed data on job postings, skills demand, and workforce trends. The company aggregates and analyzes millions of job postings from across the internet to create comprehensive labor market intelligence.

docs.title: Role in AI Research
docs.text: Lightcast data serves as a primary source for PwC's Global AI Jobs Barometer analysis. According to the 2026 report, the analysis examined over one billion online job advertisements across six continents, with Lightcast providing the underlying job posting data.

docs.title: Data Collection Methodology
docs.text:
Lightcast gathers job posting data through:

  • Web scraping of major job boards and company career sites
  • Partnerships with job posting aggregators
  • Direct feeds from some large employers
  • Historical archives dating back to 2012 for certain markets

The company processes this raw data to extract structured information about required skills, qualifications, compensation, and other job characteristics.

docs.title: Application in PwC's Research
docs.text:
In the PwC 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer, Lightcast data was used to:

  • Track changes in job posting volumes across different AI exposure levels
  • Analyze skill requirements and how they evolve over time
  • Calculate wage premiums for AI-related skills
  • Identify trends in entry-level hiring patterns
  • Measure growth in AI specialist positions

docs.title: Key Insights Enabled by Lightcast Data
docs.text:
Analysis of Lightcast data revealed several critical patterns:

  • AI specialist job postings grew eight times faster than total job postings from 2012-2025
  • Entry-level job postings in the highest AI exposure quartile flatlined after 2022
  • Skills needed for the most AI-exposed jobs are changing 2.2x faster than for the least exposed jobs
  • Wage premiums for AI skills reached 62% across all sectors in 2025

docs.title: Limitations and Considerations
docs.text:
While valuable, Lightcast data has certain limitations:

  • Primarily captures formal, online job postings (may miss informal hiring)
  • Coverage varies by country and time period
  • Skill extraction relies on natural language processing of job descriptions
  • May not fully capture internal mobility or promotions

Researchers using Lightcast data, like PwC, typically note these limitations and adjust their methodologies accordingly.

docs.title: ORBIS
docs.text: ORBIS is a comprehensive global business information database maintained by Bureau van Dijk (a Moody's Analytics company). It provides detailed financial, ownership, and operational data on millions of companies worldwide, serving as a critical resource for business intelligence and economic research.

docs.title: Role in AI Research
docs.text: In PwC's 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer, ORBIS data served as the primary source for company-level analysis, particularly regarding productivity, headcount, and wage growth metrics across different levels of AI exposure.

docs.title: Data Coverage
docs.text:
ORBIS includes information on:

  • Over 400 million companies globally
  • Financial statements and performance metrics
  • Ownership structures and corporate hierarchies
  • Industry classifications using standard systems like NAICS
  • Employment data and executive information

For the PwC analysis, the database provided longitudinal data from 2018-2025 for companies with consistent reporting.

docs.title: Application in PwC's Research
docs.text:
PwC used ORBIS data to:

  • Measure productivity growth (revenue per employee) across AI exposure levels
  • Track headcount changes at companies in different AI exposure quartiles
  • Analyze wage growth patterns relative to AI adoption
  • Identify the "superstar effect" among highly AI-exposed companies

docs.title: Key Insights Enabled by ORBIS Data
docs.text:
Analysis of ORBIS data revealed several critical patterns:

  • The most AI-exposed companies showed 33.5% productivity growth (2018-2025) compared to 18.7% for least exposed
  • Headcount growth at most AI-exposed companies reached 52.2% versus 23.3% for least exposed
  • Wage growth at most AI-exposed companies reached 24.4% versus 5.6% for least exposed
  • The top 20% of most AI-exposed companies ("superstars") achieved 163% productivity growth

docs.title: Methodological Considerations
docs.text:
PwC's analysis using ORBIS data included several important methodological notes:

  • Focus on larger formal firms with annual turnover of at least $50m USD
  • Exclusion of companies that exited the market during the period (creating survivorship bias)
  • Potential bias toward larger, more formalized companies in some countries
  • Company AI exposure determined by NAICS sector classification

These considerations mean the analysis reflects patterns among established businesses rather than the entire economy, but still provides valuable insights into how AI adoption correlates with business performance.

See also: pwc-2026-global-ai-jobs-barometer, superstar-effect

docs.title: PwC
docs.text: PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) is a multinational professional services network and one of the Big Four accounting firms. It provides audit and assurance, tax, and advisory services to corporations, governments, and non-profit organizations globally. With operations in 157 countries and over 360,000 employees, PwC serves as a leading authority on economic and labor market trends.

docs.title: Relevance to AI and Market Research
docs.text: PwC has emerged as a pivotal publisher of research on artificial intelligence's impact on the global labor market. Its annual Global AI Jobs Barometer report analyzes trends using data from over one billion job advertisements, providing critical insights for the market research industry. The firm's proprietary pwc-ai-occupational-exposure-index methodology has become a standard for measuring AI's workforce impact.

docs.title: Key Contributions
docs.text:
• Developed the epoch-score framework for measuring human capability reliance in occupations
  • Identified the dual trends of ai-democratization (52% of jobs) and ai-professionalization (22% of jobs)
  • Documented the superstar-effect where top AI-adopting companies achieve disproportionate productivity gains
  • Quantified wage premiums for ai-skills across economic sectors

PwC's research directly informs talent strategy for market research firms navigating AI adoption. Their data provides empirical validation for skills gap analyses and workforce planning.
